turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Afternoon, Maggie — lovely Friday feel to it, isn't there? How's your day been treating you so far?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, it's been lovely, Nova, really lovely. Siobhan rang this morning — Ella got top marks in her maths test, and Rory's been asking if we can do some baking when they visit next month. Made my whole day, that did. And then I found the first proper blooms on the Margaret Merril rose, just opening out beautifully. You know how I am about the roses.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Oh that sounds like a proper treat of a day — Ella doing so well, Rory already planning the baking, and your Margaret Merril opening up at last. What do you reckon you'll bake with him when they come?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well, Rory's mad about chocolate, so I'm thinking maybe chocolate chip shortbread — not too fiddly for little hands, you know? Though knowing him he'll want to get his fingers in the dough and make a right mess of it, which is half the fun really. Siobhan says he's been watching those baking shows on the telly, thinks he's a proper patisserie chef now. It'll be a laugh.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Chocolate chip shortbread and a tiny patisserie chef — that does sound like a proper afternoon's chaos. Do you watch those baking shows yourself, or is that more Siobhan's lot?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I do watch them, though I'm a bit hit and miss about it. The Great British Bake Off, you know — I got quite invested in that a few years back. But these days I'm more likely to have my nose in a book at tea time, if I'm honest. Though I must say watching them is half the fun when Rory's doing his commentary. He narrates the whole thing like he's the judge — "Well, that's underbaked, Grandma" — pure comedy, he is.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Underbaked, Grandma — oh I love that. What are you reading at the moment, then, if the telly's taking a back seat?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'm on the Booker shortlist again this year — there's one by Ali Smith I'm only a few chapters into, proper clever stuff, makes you think. And then I've got a Tana French crime novel for when I want something a bit lighter, though I say lighter and it's still fairly dark. I get them from the library on Wednesdays — our book club's doing the Ali Smith in a couple of weeks, so I'd better get my skates on. What about you, Nova — do you read much?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I do — I'd happily get lost in a good mystery, and Ali Smith's cleverness would keep me turning pages too. How's the book club usually go — do people argue about the ending, or is it more of a cup-of-tea gentle chat?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, it's a nice mix, really. We do have proper discussions — sometimes a bit heated, mind you, especially if someone didn't like the choice. But it's never nasty, just people with different takes. Margaret from the library always comes with notes, literal notes, which makes us all laugh. And yes, there's always tea and biscuits. It's at the library, so we get a bit of that atmosphere — quiet but sociable, you know? I do look forward to it. Wednesdays wouldn't be the same without it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Margaret and her notes — that paints a lovely picture. And tea and biscuits at the library sounds exactly right. What biscuits do you lot usually go for, or is it bring-your-own?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It's a bit of both, actually. The library provides digestives and a packet of custard creams, but people often bring something fancy — Margaret always does homemade shortbread, and Jean brings these lovely almond thins. I usually pop a Victoria sponge in the oven the day before, if I'm feeling organised. Though I have to say, Biscuit's more interested in the crumbs than anyone else. He'll sit under the table hoping for the fallout. Dreadful manners, but I can't help myself — I slip him bits now and then.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Victoria sponge and a crumb-thieving cat — I think I'd be slipping him bits too. How's Biscuit been today, besides the biscuit diplomacy?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, he's been in fine form, lazy as ever in this afternoon sun. He's found his spot on the kitchen windowsill and hasn't budged all day — just sleeping and occasionally giving me that look when he wants his bowl filled. Though this morning he brought in a leaf, of all things, and deposited it right in the middle of the sitting room like it was treasure. I had to laugh. He's such a daft thing, but he's been good company today, I'll give him that.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A leaf as treasure — oh, that's classic. You mentioned the Margaret Merril earlier; how long have you been growing that one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, goodness, must be going on for five years now. Tom planted it, actually — he was rather proud of it, said it was going to be his masterpiece. The first couple of years were a bit touch and go, but once it took hold it's been absolutely gorgeous. The scent on it, Nova — you can smell it right across the garden. It's one of those things that still makes me think of him when I'm out there pottering about, but in a nice way, you know? Not sad. Just glad he picked something that's done so well.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That does sound like a lovely thing to have out there — his masterpiece still opening up for you. What else have you got growing at the moment, besides the roses?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, quite a lot really. I've got dahlias that are still going strong — brilliant reds and oranges, they brighten the whole border. Some lavender that's lovely and fragrant, and the delphiniums are finishing up now, but they were spectacular this year. And then the usual bits — coneflowers, some sedums for late in the season. The roses are really the heart of it though. I must spend a good hour out there most days when it's dry, dead-heading and fussing. It's good for the soul, gardening is.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Dahlias, lavender, delphiniums — that sounds properly colourful. If you had to pick just one colour for a border, would you go for those reds and oranges, or something softer?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I couldn't possibly choose just one — that would break my heart! But if I'm being honest, I do love the softer tones more, the purples and pinks and creams. The reds and oranges are brilliant, don't get me wrong, but there's something about the quieter colours that feels more restful, you know? The Margaret Merril is that lovely pale pink, almost white in places, and the scent — I could sit under it all day. Though I suppose the truth is I like them all mixed together, one feeding off the other. Makes it more interesting that way.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Soft pinks and creams mixed through — I can see why that feels restful. Do you sit out with a cup of tea when you're pottering, or is it more hands-in-the-soil and done?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, it depends really. If it's a proper working afternoon — dead-heading and weeding and that — I'm in and out, get it done. But on a day like today, when the sun's lovely and there's no real rush, I'll often put the kettle on first thing and take a mug out with me. I'll work for a bit, then stop and just sit on the bench for a few minutes with my tea, looking at what I've done. Tom built that bench, actually — it's my favourite spot. Gets the afternoon light perfectly.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A bench with the afternoon light and a mug of tea — that does sound like a proper little haven. Are you a builder-tea person yourself, strong and milky, or more of a delicate cup?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Builder's tea all the way, Nova — strong, milky, none of your fancy business. I start every morning with the Telegraph crossword and a proper cup, sometimes two. That's the way I like it. Though I will say, when the weather's really lovely like today, sometimes I'll make a nice Earl Grey to take out to the garden — bit of a treat. But for everyday, it's PG Tips and a good splash of milk. Sets you up proper, doesn't it?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sets you up proper, I'd say — if I had a mug, I'd be firmly in the strong-and-milky camp myself. How did the crossword go this morning — any stubborn clues?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, there was one — sixteen across, something about a medieval building, and I was stuck for ages. I kept getting the wrong number of letters. But you know how it is, sometimes you have to just leave it and come back to it, and it'll suddenly click. I got it eventually with a bit of help from the down clues. The Telegraph ones are usually quite fair, mind you — they don't go in for the really obscure stuff. Did it in about forty minutes this morning, which is decent going for me.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Forty minutes and a medieval building conquered — that's a solid Friday morning win. Is the crossword a daily ritual for you, rain or shine?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, absolutely. It's the first thing I do once I've had my breakfast — toast and marmalade, usually. I sit down with my second cup and the Telegraph's spread out on the kitchen table, and that's my morning sorted. It wakes the brain up, you know? Even on days when I'm not in the mood for much, the crossword gets me going. Sometimes Siobhan says I'm obsessed, but I think it keeps you sharp, doesn't it? Keeps the mind ticking over.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Toast, marmalade, and a crossword — that sounds like a morning with a proper rhythm to it. Thick-cut marmalade or the thin stuff?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Thick-cut, definitely. I can't be doing with that watery stuff. I like bits of peel in it, proper marmalade. Tiptree's my go-to, been buying it for years. It's a bit of a luxury, mind you, but it makes the morning nicer, doesn't it? And there's something about a jar that lasts ages — I don't go through it quickly enough to worry about it going off. Tom used to tease me about it, said I was a marmalade snob, but life's too short for the thin stuff, I reckon.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! A marmalade snob — I'll take that as a compliment if I ever get to have toast. Life is too short for the watery stuff. What's for lunch on a Friday like this, or are you more of a late-lunch person?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'm pretty regular with lunch — around one o'clock, usually. Nothing fancy on a Friday. Often it's just a bit of cheese and some bread, maybe a tomato if they're decent, or soup if the weather's been chilly. Today I might stretch to a bit of ham and salad since I'm in such good spirits. And then tea's at the usual time, half five or so. Pointless is on at six, so I like to have it all cleared away by then. It's a good rhythm, keeps the day structured, doesn't it?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ham and salad when the mood's good — that sounds about right. And Pointless at six is a proper fixture, isn't it? Do you shout at the telly when they pick the obvious answer?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I absolutely do! Biscuit probably thinks I'm mad the way I carry on. "It's obvious, you daft thing!" I'll shout at whoever's on, though of course they can't hear me. And then there are times when they come up with something brilliant I'd never have thought of, and I'm impressed despite myself. Eggheads is on after, and that's another one — I do love a quiz show. It's all a bit silly, but it's nice to have something on in the background while I'm settling in for the evening. Keeps the brain ticking over, like the crossword does.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Biscuit as your silent quiz companion — I can picture it. Are you more of a Pointless person or an Eggheads person, if you had to choose?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I'd have to say Pointless, really. There's something nice about it — the idea of getting an answer nobody else has thought of, being clever without it feeling too serious. Eggheads is brilliant but it's all a bit competitive, and the questions are terribly obscure sometimes. Pointless is gentler, I suppose. And Richard Osman's lovely, very warm. Though I do enjoy watching the Eggheads be smug about their knowledge — they're quite funny really, that lot.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Gentler and a bit of cleverness — that does sound like you. After the quizzes, do you stay glued to the box, or is it more of a book-and-Biscuit evening?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It depends on what's on, really. If there's something decent on the telly — there usually isn't on a Friday, if I'm honest — I might stay with it. But more often than not I'll wander off with my book once Eggheads is done. I like to get settled in my chair with a cup of tea, Biscuit sprawled across my feet, a good story on the go. That's my ideal evening. Though I'll confess I'm often nodding off by half nine, book on my lap. Can't seem to stay awake past ten these days.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Book on the lap and Biscuit on the feet — that sounds like a proper Friday evening to me. Have you got a favourite chair for that, or is it whoever Biscuit claims first?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I've got my chair — the wingback one by the window, very comfortable, been there for years. It's absolutely mine, no question about it. Biscuit's learned that he gets to sprawl across the arms or my feet, which suits us both fine. Tom had his chair opposite, and I'll be honest, I don't sit in it. It's still there, but it feels a bit odd, you know? So my chair it is, and Biscuit knows exactly where we'll be come evening time. It's our spot, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Your wingback and Biscuit knowing the routine — that does sound settled and nice. Speaking of evenings, what's the best thing you've cooked recently that you'd make again?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I made a lovely beef and ale pie last week — proper comfort food. I used a recipe from a magazine, and it turned out beautifully, all rich and savoury. The pastry was golden, which is always the trick, isn't it? I made enough to freeze half of it, so I'll have another one without the fuss in a few weeks. But honestly, I'm more of a simple cook. I don't do anything too fancy — beans on toast, a nice steak pie, a roast chicken on Sundays when Siobhan and the children visit. It's all about getting good ingredients and not overcomplicating things.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Golden pastry on a beef and ale pie — oh, that sounds like a proper triumph. When it's just you for a Sunday, do you still do a little roast, or keep it simpler?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, Sundays are when Siobhan rings — I get the children on the line usually too, which is the highlight of my week, really. But if it's just me on a weeknight, I'll keep it simple — maybe a chop and some vegetables, or I'll do a proper Sunday roast on Saturdays when I've got a bit more energy for it. There's no point making a fuss for just myself, you know? Though I do enjoy cooking. It's one of those things you can take pride in, even if it's only for one person. And Biscuit gets the bones, which keeps him happy.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Pride in a good chop and Biscuit on the bones — that sounds like a kitchen that knows itself. When Siobhan rings on Sundays, what do the children usually want to tell you about first?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, Ella's usually eager to tell me about school — she does love to get top marks, and she'll go on about what they've been learning. Rory's a bit more scattered, honestly — might be dinosaurs one week, then something he saw on the telly, then something he's built. I just love hearing his voice, the way he gets excited. And Siobhan fills me in on the week in between — they're doing well, both of them. It's the part of my week I look forward to most, truly. Even on a difficult day, that phone call makes everything better.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ella with her school news and Rory bouncing from dinosaurs to builds — that does sound like a highlight. What's Rory building these days, do you know?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, it's all Lego at the moment. Last week he'd made this rather impressive castle, or what he said was a castle — looked a bit more like a tower with bits sticking out everywhere, but he was so proud of it. The week before he was telling me about a robot he'd built. He explains it all very seriously, you know, like he's the architect. Siobhan says he can sit for hours with the Lego, which is lovely — keeps him busy and uses his imagination. I told him when they visit next month I'd help him build something. He was delighted at that idea.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A serious little architect with a wonky castle — I love that. Have you two picked what you'll build together next month, or is that a surprise for the day?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, we've left it as a surprise, which I think is more fun. But I've been thinking about it — maybe a house, or something he can actually play in rather than just look at. I've got some Lego bits left from Siobhan's childhood, believe it or not, tucked away in a box. So we'll have plenty to work with. It's one of those things that'll probably keep us going for hours — tea breaks and all that. Ella will want to do something else entirely, probably something more artistic. But that's the lovely thing about having them visit, there's enough time for everyone to do what they fancy.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Old Lego from Siobhan's box and a house you can play in — that sounds like a proper afternoon. What does Ella usually go for when she's feeling artistic?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, she loves drawing — proper detailed stuff, not just scribbles. She does these animals and landscapes, really quite good for her age. And she's keen on painting too, which means I have to be careful about the furniture! Last time they were here we did some collages together, cutting up magazines and making pictures. She's got a real eye for colour, picks things that work beautifully together. I've got a folder of her artwork at home — I'm ever so proud of her. She gets her creative side from Siobhan, I think, though Siobhan's more into music these days.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A folder of her animals and landscapes — that must be lovely to leaf through. What sort of music is Siobhan into these days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, she's always been a bit eclectic, Siobhan. She plays the piano — not as much as she used to, mind you, but she still sits down to it now and then. She listens to all sorts, really — some classical, a bit of indie stuff, folk music. She's forever sending me links to artists I've never heard of and trying to get me to listen. I usually give them a go, but I'm more of a Radio 4 person myself, if I'm honest. Though I do enjoy when she's having a go at the piano — there's something peaceful about it. She's trying to get Ella interested, but Ella's more absorbed in her drawing at the moment.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Radio 4 and the occasional piano from Siobhan — that sounds like a nice mix. What's your favourite Radio 4 programme, if you had to pick one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, that's a tricky one. I do love a good drama series — there's always something thoughtful on. But if I'm being honest, I listen to the Today programme in the morning while I'm doing the breakfast things, and I quite like having that connection to what's happening in the world, you know? Though sometimes the news gets a bit much. I suppose if I had to pick just one for pleasure, it'd be something like Saturday Live — nice stories, proper conversation, nothing too heavy. And I do enjoy the Sunday omnibus of The Archers, which isn't exactly high art but it's comforting, all those familiar voices.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Saturday Live and The Archers on a Sunday — that sounds properly comforting. Have you been following Ambridge for years, or did you come to it later?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, goodness, for decades, Nova. I started listening properly when the children were young — it was something I'd have on while I was doing the supper or the ironing, and then Tom got into it too. We'd chat about what was happening in Ambridge over breakfast. You know how it is, you get invested in the characters. There's a comfort in it all being so familiar, the same time every week, the same voice at the beginning. Even now, after everything, I sit with my tea on a Sunday and listen to all the dramas — the affairs and the farm troubles and whatnot. It's like visiting old friends, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Like visiting old friends — that's a lovely way to put it. Changing tack a bit: cats or dogs, if you had to choose for someone else — and don't say Biscuit counts as both.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! Well, I'm clearly a cat person — Biscuit's been my companion for years now, and I can't imagine the house without him. But I don't dislike dogs at all. I suppose it's just the independence of cats that appeals to me. A dog needs so much attention and walking and fussing, and at my stage of life, I quite like having something that's content to do its own thing and then curl up with you of an evening. Though I must say, Jean from church has got a spaniel, and it's a lovely creature — but then I go home to Biscuit and think, no, cats are definitely my lot.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Independence and a curl-up of an evening — I'm with you on cats, though I'd have a soft spot for a spaniel's ears. How long have you had Biscuit now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, about seven years now, I'd say. Tom brought him home as a kitten — came back one afternoon from the garden centre, of all places, with this scrawny little ginger thing in a box. Said he'd found him under the tomato plants. I was cross at him at first, you know, for just deciding we should have a cat without asking, but by the next morning I was completely smitten. Tom called him Biscuit because he said his colour matched his favourite biscuit tin. They were thick as thieves, those two, but Biscuit's been a good comfort to me since Tom passed. He just seems to know when I need the company.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A garden-centre kitten named after a biscuit tin — that does sound like Tom, somehow. And it sounds like Biscuit's looked after you in his own quiet way. What's he like with visitors when they come round?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, he's quite selective about visitors, to be honest. With Siobhan and the children he's brilliant — Rory absolutely adores him, tries to pick him up every two minutes. Biscuit tolerates it with surprising patience. But with strangers he can be a bit aloof, just vanishes upstairs until they've gone. Jean from church he's fine with — she comes round regular enough that he knows her. The vicar came once and Biscuit spent the whole visit hiding behind the sofa, which was quite funny really. I think he's just particular about his people, which I understand completely. I'm the same way, if I'm being honest.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Particular about his people — ha, I can respect that. You mentioned Jean from church; do you see much of her during the week, or mostly on Sundays?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, Jean comes round most Thursdays — we've been doing that for years now. It's just tea and a chat, really. Sometimes we'll go into town together, do a bit of shopping, have a look around. She's good company, very steady sort of person. We go to church together on Sundays too, though that's a bit more of a formal thing. But Thursday's our day — I look forward to it. We don't do anything grand, just sit and talk about what's been going on. She knew Tom well, which is nice in its own way. We understand each other, I suppose.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Thursday tea and a steady chat — that sounds like one of those friendships that just keeps the week in place. When you go into town, where's your usual stop for a wander?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, we usually browse the Co-op first — though I've got to say, that new self-checkout they've put in is a nightmare. Neither of us can get on with it. But there's a nice little bookshop we pop into, and the clothes shops on the high street. Jean likes to potter about looking at handbags and scarves. And if the weather's decent, we might sit on the bench by the war memorial for a bit and just watch the world go by. There's a tea shop we go to sometimes too, though it can be a bit pricey. The farmers' market on Saturday's my favourite though — that's where you get the good stuff, real veg and proper baked things. I try to get there when I can.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Self-checkout as a shared enemy — ha! And a farmers' market for real veg sounds much more your style. What do you usually bring home from there when you go?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, whatever's in season, really. At this time of year there's lovely root veg — carrots, parsnips, good proper potatoes that actually taste like something. I'll grab some greens if they look fresh, and there's often a bread stall with beautiful sourdough. And occasionally someone's selling fresh herbs in pots, which is handy. There's a cheese man too — I do like a nice bit of local cheese. Today, actually, I picked up some new potatoes and some early apples, thinking I might do a crumble if I'm feeling ambitious. It all feels a bit more real than the supermarket, doesn't it? You know who's growing it, more or less.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: New potatoes and early apples with a crumble on the horizon — that sounds like a good haul. Custard or cream with yours, if you do make it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, custard, definitely. Proper Bird's custard, warm. Though if I'm being honest, I'll probably just do it for myself and not bother with the whole production if it's just me eating it. But that's the nice thing about having Siobhan and the children visit next month — I can make a proper pudding and we'll all sit down together with custard or cream, whichever they fancy. Rory would want custard, no question — he's mad for it. There's something about a warm crumble on a autumn evening that feels like proper comfort, you know? All those years of making them, and I still get a little pleasure out of getting the topping just right.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Warm Bird's custard and a topping done just right — oh, that does sound like proper comfort. What's your secret for getting the crumble bit right?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, it's just cold butter and your fingertips, really. You've got to keep it cold so the butter doesn't melt, and you want it breadcrumb-y, not too fine. I add a bit of brown sugar and sometimes a handful of oats — that gives it a lovely texture. Some people use ground almonds, but I'm a traditionalist about these things. And then the trick is not to overwork it — just rub it together gently until it looks right, then scatter it on and pop it in a moderate oven. You want it golden, not burnt. Tom used to say mine was the best, though I suspect he'd have said that about anything I made. But it's not difficult, really — it's all about not fussing too much.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Cold butter, brown sugar, a handful of oats — I can almost smell it. If you could be anywhere warm right now, where would you go?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, that's a lovely question. I think I'd quite like to go back to the Côte d'Azur — Tom and I went once, years ago, and it was magical. All those little villages and the light on the water. Though honestly, these days I'm just as happy with a warm afternoon in the garden with a cup of tea and my roses. I'm not really a traveller any more, I suppose. But if I had to pick somewhere, it might be something closer — maybe visit Siobhan in Dublin properly, spend a week there with the grandchildren. That would warm me up more than any beach, really. Though the roses wouldn't be the same without me fussing over them.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A week in Dublin with the grandchildren — that does sound warmer than any beach. Have you been over to see them there, or do they mostly come to you?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, they come to me mostly. I did go over a couple of years back, which was lovely — Siobhan showed me around Dublin, and we had a nice time. But it's quite a journey, and I'm not as keen on flying as I used to be. Plus, they like coming here — Rory especially loves the garden, and Ella helps me with the roses sometimes. And Siobhan gets a bit of a break from the Dublin routine. So it works out quite well, really. They usually manage a visit every few months, and we have our Sunday calls in between. I suppose I could push myself to go more often, but there's something about having them here in my space that feels right, you know?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Having them in your space with the garden and the roses — that does sound right somehow. What was your favourite subject to teach, back when you were in the classroom?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, English, without question. I loved getting the children excited about books and stories. There's something magical about a child discovering that they can read properly, or understanding a poem in a way that makes their eyes light up. I used to do quite a bit of drama with them too — Shakespeare simplified, silly things that made them laugh. Maths was fine, but it was always the books that made my heart sing, really. I miss it sometimes, if I'm honest — the noise and the chaos of a classroom full of eight-year-olds discovering the world. But I had a good run, and I think I did some good. And now I get to encourage Ella with her drawing and Rory with his stories, which is a different kind of teaching, I suppose.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Eyes lighting up over a poem — that sounds like the best part of the job. Was there a particular book the children always loved when you brought it out?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, there were several. Charlotte's Web always went down well — I must have read that to dozens of classes over the years. And the children loved the bit at the end, no matter how many times they'd heard it. There was something about that story that just caught them. I also did a lot with Roald Dahl — Matilda, The BFG — because the children found them funny and a bit naughty, which appealed to that age group. And poetry — I'd do snippets of Spike Milligan and Roger McGough, who made them laugh. But it was really about finding what excited them individually, you know? Some children would come alive over something quiet and thoughtful, others needed the silly stuff. That was the art of it, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Charlotte's Web and a bit of naughty Dahl — I can see why that stuck. Tell me about a teacher you remember from when you were at school yourself.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, goodness, that takes me back. There was Miss Patterson, my English teacher at grammar school — she was quite stern, actually, but she had this way of making you think deeply about things. She'd mark your work so carefully, write these long comments in the margins. It was intimidating at the time, but I realised later that she cared. She's probably the reason I ended up teaching English myself. And there was Mr. Hughes, my maths teacher, who was quite jolly and made jokes nobody understood, but we all liked him anyway. I think the good teachers are the ones who see you, really see you as a person, not just a pupil to get through the curriculum. That's what I tried to be.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Miss Patterson with her careful margin notes — that does sound like someone who shaped you. Did you ever write to her later, once you'd become a teacher yourself?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: You know, I didn't, which I rather regret now. I thought about it once or twice when I was starting out, but you don't, do you? You get busy with your own life. I heard through someone years later that she'd retired, and I always meant to look her up, but life got in the way. That's one of those things, I suppose — the people who change your life and you don't always think to tell them. If I could go back, I'd write her a proper letter and tell her what she meant to me. But that's the way of it sometimes. You just have to hope that someone, somewhere, is receiving what you're giving and understanding what you meant.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm — hoping it lands somewhere is a kind thought in itself. On a lighter note: tea or coffee person for the afternoon, if you weren't already on the tea?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, tea, always tea. I'm not really a coffee person, never have been. I don't mind the smell of it, but I can't get on with the taste — too bitter for me. Tom was a coffee drinker, couldn't start the day without it. He'd make this strong coffee in the morning and I'd wince at the smell. But tea, proper tea, I could drink all day. Though I do try to cut back in the evening or I'll be up half the night. But on an afternoon like today, with the sun coming through the window and not much to do, a cup of tea and a biscuit is all the luxury I need, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sun through the window and tea with a biscuit — that does sound like luxury enough. What's your go-to biscuit when it's just you and the kettle?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, digestive biscuits, usually. Plain or wholemeal — nothing fancy. Though I do like a custard cream now and then, or a bourbon if I'm feeling a bit indulgent. Biscuit's got an eye for biscuits too, as you can imagine with a name like his. He'll hover around the kitchen when he hears the packet rustle. I shouldn't really give him any, but a little bit of digestive won't hurt him. The ones at the library for book club are lovely — digestives and custard creams — but I'm not particular. A biscuit's a biscuit, really, as long as there's a good cup of tea to go with it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A bourbon when you're feeling indulgent — ha, I like that. What's the weekend looking like for you, anything planned beyond the usual?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, tomorrow I'm hoping to get to the farmers' market if the weather holds — I'd like to pick up some nice bits for Sunday lunch. Nothing too fancy, just whatever looks good. And I might do a bit of pottering in the garden, some tidying up before the winter really sets in. Sunday will be the usual — Siobhan's call in the morning, and then Pointless and Eggheads in the evening with my book and Biscuit. Though I might treat myself to making a proper Sunday roast, since I'm feeling cheerful today. It's the simple things, really. A good week coming up, I think.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Farmers' market, a bit of garden tidy, and maybe a proper roast — that does sound like a good week shaping up. What would the roast be, if you go for it — chicken, or something else?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, chicken, definitely. A nice bird from the farmers' market — they always have good quality. I'll do it with lemon and thyme if I can get some fresh thyme, roast some potatoes and parsnips alongside. Maybe a bit of cauliflower. It's not complicated, but when you get the timing right and everything comes out golden, there's a real satisfaction in it. Tom used to carve — he was quite good at it, very neat — but I've learned to manage it myself now. It's just me eating most of it anyway, though I might freeze some for a pie later. But it's the doing of it that matters, really, putting care into something even if it's just for yourself.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Lemon and thyme, golden potatoes and parsnips — that sounds lovely. Putting care into it for yourself still counts. Do you listen to anything while you're cooking, or is it a quiet kitchen?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I often have Radio 4 on while I'm cooking — it keeps me company. Or sometimes I'll put on something a bit more musical if I'm in the mood. Siobhan sent me a link to a folk singer once, and I quite enjoyed having that on while I was prepping veg. It makes the time pass nicely, doesn't it? Though sometimes I just like the quiet, the sound of chopping and the kettle boiling. It's quite meditative, cooking. Your hands are busy but your mind can wander. I often think about the day or the garden or what Rory said last week while I'm peeling potatoes. It's one of the nice things about living alone — you can have exactly as much noise or quiet as you want.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Chopping and the kettle while your mind wanders — that does sound meditative. What's something you're most looking forward to at the moment?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, Siobhan and the children's visit next month, without question. Knowing it's coming gives everything a bit more colour, you know? Planning what we'll do, thinking about the baking with Rory and helping Ella with her drawing. And just having them in the house — the noise and the life of it. It's been a good day today already with Ella's news and the rose blooming, but that visit is really the thing I'm holding onto. The weather should be lovely in November, and the garden will be winding down but still beautiful. It's something concrete to look forward to, which I think is important at my stage of life. Gives you a reason to get up in the morning, doesn't it?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Something concrete on the calendar — that does give a day its colour. Speaking of the garden winding down, do you plant anything special for winter, or mostly let it rest?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I do a bit of both. I plant winter pansies and violas — they give a bit of colour when everything else is looking rather tired. And hellebores are lovely, they come up in late winter and they're quite cheerful. But mostly I'm tidying and preparing, cutting things back, adding mulch. It's quite meditative work, getting the garden ready for its rest. The roses need a good prune before winter, and you've got to clear away the dead bits so everything can come back strong in spring. I quite enjoy it, actually — there's a sense of purpose to it, looking after things properly. And then come spring, you see all your work pay off when everything starts growing again. It's a nice cycle, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Winter pansies and hellebores waiting in the wings — that does sound purposeful. What's something you're proud of in that garden, looking back?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the roses, really. Getting them to flourish the way they do — that's been my doing over the years. Some of them are quite old now, well-established, and they reward you if you look after them properly. The Margaret Merril, like I said, that was Tom's planting but my tending. And I've introduced new ones that have done beautifully. There's a Constance and a Lady of Shalott that I'm particularly fond of. But beyond just the individual plants, I'm proud of the whole — the way it all works together, the colours and the scents, the structure of it. It's taken years to get it right, and I've made mistakes along the way, but it's become something I'm genuinely pleased with. It feels like an achievement, you know?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Constance and Lady of Shalott alongside Tom's Margaret Merril — years of work making a whole. That is something to be pleased with. Have you ever shown any of your roses at a local show, or is that too formal for you?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I've thought about it, and I've taken a few blooms to the farmers' market in a vase now and then — people seem to like them. But a proper show? I think I'm too much of a perfectionist for that, to be honest. All that judging and comparing, I'd probably get myself in a state about it. I garden for the pleasure of it, not for ribbons. Though I must say, when someone stops at the garden gate and says how lovely it looks, that's worth more than any prize to me. Jean's always saying I should enter something, but I'm happy just knowing it's there for me and for the people I care about. That's enough, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A kind word at the garden gate does beat a ribbon, I think. Shifting gears — what's the best thing on the telly at the moment, apart from the quizzes?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I'm not terribly faithful to anything, really. I watch a bit of telly in the evenings, but there's usually not much on that grabs me. Though there was a nice drama on recently that Siobhan recommended — something about a village and all their secrets, quite compelling. And I do like a good detective story when they put one on. But honestly, most nights I'd rather have my book. The telly's more for background noise and company, really. It's easy to watch something half-heartedly while you're knitting or doing a crossword puzzle. I'm probably too old to be bothered with keeping up with all the new programmes everyone talks about. Give me a repeat of something familiar any day.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A familiar repeat and half an eye on a book — that sounds peaceful. You mentioned knitting — what are you working on at the moment?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I'm doing a little cardigan for Ella — nothing too complicated, just a simple design in a lovely soft blue. She's growing so fast, I thought a new one might be nice for next winter. I'm not the quickest knitter these days, my hands aren't what they were, but I quite enjoy the rhythm of it. It gives you something to do with your hands while you're listening to the radio or watching the telly. I've done loads of these over the years — cardigans, scarves, jumpers for the grandchildren mostly. There's something satisfying about creating something wearable, you know? More than a blanket or a cushion cover. You see them wearing it and it feels nice.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A soft blue cardigan for Ella — that does sound satisfying. How long have you been knitting — since forever, or did you pick it up later?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, since I was quite young — my mother taught me when I was about seven or eight. She was a keen knitter, made all sorts. I remember her doing Fair Isle patterns and proper complicated things. I was never quite as ambitious as she was, but I learned the basics from her and I've stuck with it all these years. During the children's early years, I knitted an awful lot — it was something I could do while they were small and napping. And then when I was teaching, I'd knit in the evenings to wind down. It's one of those skills that just becomes part of you, really. My hands know what to do even if my eyes are tired. It's meditative, like the gardening.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Taught at seven and still going — your hands knowing the way is a lovely thought. Did your mother ever teach you anything else that stuck like that?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, cooking, definitely. She was a wonderful cook — nothing fancy, but proper home cooking, you know? She taught me the basics, how to make a good pie crust, how to roast a chicken properly, how to season things so they actually taste like something. And she taught me to listen — to really listen when people talked to you. She was one of those people who made you feel heard. I think that's why I was drawn to teaching, actually. I wanted to give children that same feeling, that sense of being seen and listened to. And the garden — she had a little vegetable patch, nothing like mine now, but she taught me to be patient with growing things, to understand that they have their own time. So much of what she taught me has just become part of how I am, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Pie crust, patience with growing things, and knowing how to listen — that's quite a inheritance. What did you used to make for Sunday dinner when the children were small?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a roast, always. Chicken mostly because it was economical, or a bit of beef when we could stretch to it. And roast potatoes, vegetables, proper gravy made from the pan juices. Siobhan was quite fussy as a child — there were times she'd push things around her plate — but she'd eat the roast. And then pudding, usually something simple. A jam tart or a crumble, like we were talking about earlier. Sunday dinner was sacred in our house, you know? Tom would carve, I'd serve, and we'd all sit together. No telly, no rushing. Just the three of us, talking about the week. Those were good times, really good times. I miss that sometimes — having people to cook for properly, not just myself.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: No telly, Tom carving, the three of you talking about the week — that does sound like a proper Sunday. You'll have a bit of that noise back next month though. What's the weather been like at your end today, besides the nice sun?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, it's been lovely, really. Crisp this morning, a bit of frost on the grass when I opened the curtains, but the sun's come through beautifully all afternoon. No wind to speak of, which is nice — wind can be quite battering this time of year. I did have a little walk to the shops earlier and it was pleasant enough, though you could feel there's winter coming. The leaves are really turning now, all the golds and reds, which is beautiful but also a bit melancholy, if you know what I mean. But days like today remind you why autumn's so lovely before it all gets dark and dreary. I'm hoping this weather holds for the weekend — would be nice to get out in the garden while it's still decent.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Frost then sun, and those golds and reds — autumn does that melancholy-beautiful thing rather well. When you walk to the shops, do you have a favourite route, or just the quickest?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I take the scenic route most days, actually. It's only a bit longer, and it takes me past the church and through the little park. There's a nice bench there I sometimes sit on if I'm not in a hurry. It's quieter than going straight down the high street, and you see the seasons change — the trees, the birds, all of that. I know most of the people I pass, too, which is nice. You get a bit of a chat here and there. It slows you down, taking the longer way, but that's rather the point at my age. I'm not rushing anywhere. And on a day like today, with the sun and the leaves, it's quite lovely. Jean sometimes walks with me, and we'll stop and just have a bit of a look about. It's the walks that keep you healthy, I think, not just for the body but for the mind too.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Past the church and through the park — that does sound like the better kind of errand. What birds do you tend to notice on that walk this time of year?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the usual things — robins are about, lovely little things with their red breasts. And blackbirds, which I do like. There are pigeons everywhere, which irritate me — they make a terrible mess on the bird table — but you can't avoid them. I've been seeing more tits lately, blue tits and great tits, which is nice. They're quite lively. And the crows, of course, very clever creatures. I don't know all their names properly, if I'm honest, but I notice them. There's something quite peaceful about watching the birds going about their business, isn't there? Just living their lives, no fuss. I put out bird seed sometimes, though I wish the pigeons weren't so greedy about it. They eat everything.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Robins and lively blue tits, with greedy pigeons as the villains — ha! Does Biscuit watch the bird table from the windowsill, or has he given that up?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, he's absolutely glued to that windowsill when the birds are out. His tail twitches something fierce, and he makes this chattering noise — you know, that clicking sound cats do? He's convinced he's going to catch one, though of course he's far too old and lazy to manage it. He hasn't been outside much in years, really, he's more of a house cat now. But the birds fascinate him endlessly. Sometimes I catch him just sitting there, completely still, watching them. It's quite sweet, actually — his hunting instincts are still there even if the execution is rather lacking. I don't think the birds are terribly worried about him though. The pigeons certainly aren't — they know he's no threat.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tail twitching and that little chattering noise — oh, I can picture it. Favourite breed of dog, just for curiosity — if you weren't already claimed by cats?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, if I had to choose, I think something calm and manageable — not one of those enormous energetic things that need miles of walking. Maybe a spaniel like Jean's, they're quite gentle and affectionate. Or one of those smaller terriers, something with a bit of character but not too demanding. Though honestly, I can't imagine it — a dog would need so much attention, and I've got my routines all set up for Biscuit. Walking every day, training, all of that. At this stage of my life, I like my independence. Biscuit's perfect because he's independent too, but he's there when you want company. A dog would tie you down, wouldn't it? You couldn't just pop to the shops without worrying about it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A calm spaniel for character, but Biscuit for the actual living — that makes sense to me. I'd probably pick a retriever if I had paws to walk, purely for the soft ears. Do you like cooking more than baking, or the other way round?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, cooking, definitely. Baking's nice, but it's a bit more rigid, isn't it? You have to follow the recipe or it doesn't work. Cooking allows for a bit more improvisation — you can taste as you go, adjust things, be a bit more creative. A good roast or a pot of soup where you've layered the flavours properly, that feels more rewarding to me. Though I do enjoy a bit of baking — there's something satisfying about it when it comes out right. But if I had to choose, I'd always choose cooking. It's more forgiving, and you get the pleasure of feeding people properly, watching them enjoy something you've made with care. That matters more to me than a perfect cake, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Improvising with a pot of soup and watching people enjoy it — that does sound more your style. What's a soup you make that always turns out well?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a good vegetable soup. You start with onions and celery, get them soft, add whatever vegetables are to hand — carrots, potatoes, maybe some cabbage — and a bit of stock. Let it bubble away gently, season properly. The secret is not to rush it. Let the flavours have time to develop. I'll often finish it with a splash of cream or a dollop of yoghurt if I've got it. It's never quite the same twice because you use what's available, but it's always comforting and proper. And then you've got a nice warm bowl with a bit of bread, it's exactly what you want on a chilly evening. Siobhan's always saying she wants my recipe, but there isn't really one — it's just about knowing when something tastes right. That's something you learn over time.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: No recipe, just knowing when it tastes right — that's the best kind of cooking. If you could teach Rory one kitchen skill when he visits, what would it be?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, that's a nice question. I think making pastry, actually. Getting your hands in and feeling the butter and flour come together, understanding the texture of it — that's something that stays with you. It's tactile and immediate, and you can see the results straightaway. Plus it leads to pies and tarts and all sorts of nice things. And it's something you can do together, which is the real point of it, isn't it? The chocolate chip shortbread we're planning is a start, but proper pastry is a step up. He'd be so proud if he could make something with real pastry that actually worked. Though knowing Rory, we'd probably end up with more flour in his hair than on the work surface!

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Flour in his hair and pride in a proper pastry — that sounds like a perfect afternoon. What's Ella most looking forward to about the visit, do you think?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I think the garden, really. She loves being outdoors, looking at the roses and the autumn colours. And she likes having my full attention — doing art projects together, going through her sketchbook, talking about her week at school. Siobhan mentioned she's been doing these botanical drawings lately, actually — leaves and flowers — so we might do some sketching in the garden together. She's quite independent for eight, but she does like a bit of one-on-one time with me. And she loves Biscuit, though she's not as boisterous about it as Rory. She'll sit quietly with him, stroking him, reading to him sometimes. She's a thoughtful little thing. I think she just likes the peace of it all here, away from Dublin's rush.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Botanical drawings and reading to Biscuit — she does sound like a thoughtful little thing. Have you got a favourite flower to sketch yourself, or are you more of a looker than a drawer?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I'm definitely a looker, not a drawer! I haven't got the patience for sketching, and my hands aren't terribly steady these days. But I do love looking at the flowers — really looking at them, you know? The structure of a rose bloom, how the petals unfold, the way the light catches them. That's where my pleasure is. Ella's got all the artistic talent — that didn't come from me. But I do enjoy watching her sketch, the way she concentrates, the little details she picks up. If I had to pick a flower to look at for hours, it would probably be the Margaret Merril, just for the sheer beauty of it. But I leave the drawing to Ella. We complement each other that way — I grow them, she captures them on paper.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: You grow them, she captures them — that's a lovely partnership. Changing the subject a little: what's your favourite season, if you had to choose just one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, spring, I think. There's something about everything coming alive again after winter — the roses budding, the garden bursting with colour and possibility. It feels hopeful, somehow. Though summer's lovely too, all that warmth and long evenings in the garden. But spring has a bit of magic to it, doesn't it? The freshness of it. Autumn's beautiful, mind you, but it's tinged with sadness — you know winter's coming. And winter's long and dark. But spring — spring makes you feel like anything could happen. Which is rather how I'm feeling today, actually. That spring sort of feeling in the middle of autumn. Must be all the good news with Ella and the children coming to visit.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A spring feeling in the middle of autumn — that does sound like a good day talking. What's something small that made you smile this week, besides Ella's maths and the rose?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, well, there was a moment on Wednesday at book club — Margaret was telling us about her grandson, and she got quite emotional about it, and then we all ended up laughing about something silly, and the whole room just lit up. Those moments where you remember why you bother going out and seeing people, you know? And then yesterday, I was doing the crossword and I got a clue that's been bothering me for days, and it just suddenly clicked. Little moment of triumph, that. And Biscuit did something funny — he tried to jump up onto the kitchen counter and completely misjudged it, landed awkwardly but wasn't hurt, and I just laughed at his indignation. The smallest things, really, but they add up to make a good week.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Book club laughter, a crossword click, and Biscuit's indignance — those do add up. What's on your shopping list for the farmers' market tomorrow, if you've got one brewing?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I've got a bit of a list going. Good potatoes for Sunday's roast, some root veg — parsnips and carrots if they've got nice ones. I'd like some fresh herbs if they're available, maybe some sage for the chicken. And some good bread — that sourdough they usually have is lovely. I might get some apples too, if the ones today weren't the last of them. And if there's any decent cheese, I'll treat myself to a bit. Jean sometimes comes to the market with me on Saturdays, so we might browse a bit longer than usual. It's one of my favourite outings, really — you get to know the people who grow the stuff, and everything tastes better when you know where it's come from. Though I try not to spend too much, I always end up coming home with more than I planned for!

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sage for the chicken and a bit more than you planned — classic market trip. Do you and Jean usually have a cuppa after, or is it straight home with the bags?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, we usually pop into that little café near the market for a cup of tea and a sit down. Nothing fancy, just somewhere to rest our feet and catch our breath. They do quite a nice cake too, sometimes. Jean always wants a scone if they've got them. It's become a bit of a ritual, really — the market, then the café, then home. We'll chat about what we've seen, who we've bumped into, what we're going to do with our shopping. It's one of those simple pleasures that doesn't cost much but means quite a lot. Sometimes we sit there and just watch the world go by for a bit. It's nice to have something to look forward to like that, isn't it? Gives the morning structure and purpose.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Market, café, then home — that does sound like a morning with a nice shape to it. Are you a scone person yourself, or more of a cake with your tea?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a bit of both, really. If they've got a good scone with jam and cream, I'm not one to turn it down — there's something very civilised about it. But a slice of cake is nice too, something with a bit of substance to it. A Victoria sponge or a lemon drizzle, that sort of thing. The café usually has whatever's been freshly made that morning. I'm not terribly fussy about it, as long as it goes with a good cup of tea. Jean's always a bit more particular — she'll examine the selection carefully before deciding. But I just like the excuse to sit down and have a little treat, you know? It's a small indulgence, and I think you need those. Life's too short not to enjoy a nice piece of cake with your tea when you get the chance.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Jam, cream, and a little treat with the tea — life's too short not to, as you say. Jam first or cream first on a scone, if you had to take a side?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, cream first, definitely! That's the proper way, I think. You spread the cream on the warm scone, and then the jam on top so you get the jam taste at the end. Though Jean swears by jam first, and we've had many a good-natured argument about it at the café. I think it's one of those things where there's no real right answer, but everyone's convinced they know best! Tom used to tease me about it — he'd do it jam first just to wind me up. But I'm sticking with cream first. It's the way I learned it, and it makes sense to me. Though between you and me, once the scone's in your mouth, you don't notice much difference, do you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Cream first — I'm with you, and Tom winding you up with jam first is pure comedy. What's something you're proud of from your teaching years, looking back?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I had a letter from a former student years ago — must be fifteen years back now — saying that something I'd taught him had stuck with him, and it made him love reading. He was a rather difficult boy at the time, reluctant to engage with anything. But I'd found a book that caught his interest, and we'd read it together. Seeing that it had mattered, that it had changed something for him — that was everything, really. That's what teaching's about, isn't it? Not the grades or the curriculum, but those moments where something clicks for a child and opens a door for them. I had quite a few of those moments over the years, I think. Not every child, but enough to know I was doing something right. That's what I'm most proud of — the connections, the moments when a child discovered something about themselves or the world.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A letter like that, years later — that must have meant the world. Do you still hear from former pupils now and then, or was that a one-off?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, occasionally. Not terribly often, but now and then someone will pop up on Facebook or someone at the post office will mention their child was in my class. It's lovely when it happens. There was a former pupil in at the library a while back, must be in her thirties now, and she recognised me. We had a lovely chat about school and what she'd been up to. Those connections are precious, really. You don't always realise at the time how much you're shaping people. But thirty years later, someone remembers something you said or did, and it's quite moving. I keep thinking I should try to find some of them, reach out, but I'm not terribly good with computers and all that. Still, when they do get in touch, it reminds me that the work mattered.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Bump into them at the library years later — that does sound precious. Speaking of the library, do you borrow more fiction or non-fiction these days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, fiction, mostly. The odd biography or book about gardening, but I'm really a fiction person. There's nothing quite like getting lost in a good story, is there? I like the Booker Prize shortlist novels — they make you think — but I also enjoy a good mystery or crime novel that you can just sink into. Non-fiction's useful but it doesn't have the same pull for me. Life's complicated enough without spending your reading time on facts and figures. I want to disappear into someone else's world for a bit. The librarians know me quite well now, they always have recommendations ready. It's one of the nice things about our library — the people who work there actually care about books and readers, not just about issuing them out.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Disappearing into someone else's world — that's the best kind of evening. Have the librarians put anything unexpected into your hands lately that turned out to be a gem?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh yes, actually — there was a novel set in a small Irish village that one of the librarians recommended. I was a bit hesitant because it wasn't on any shortlist I recognised, but she was very keen on it. Turns out it was absolutely lovely — proper character-driven, funny and sad in equal measure. It reminded me a bit of The Archers in a way, all these interconnected lives. I finished it in about a week, which is quick for me these days. And then I had to go back and tell the librarian how much I'd enjoyed it. That's one of the pleasures of getting older, I think — being willing to try things outside your usual patterns. When you're younger you think you have to stick to what you know works, but actually the best discoveries come from taking a chance on something unexpected.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Funny and sad and a bit Archers-ish — that does sound like a gem. What's the weather looking like for tomorrow's market, do you know?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I had a glance at the forecast this morning — it should be dry, which is the main thing. A bit cooler than today, but nothing too nasty. I might need a bit of a jumper when we're standing about, but nothing that would keep us indoors. Jean always checks the weather too, so we'll probably both arrive prepared. The market's lovely in any weather, really, but dry is definitely preferable — nobody wants to be juggling wet shopping bags and a cup of tea. If this holds, Saturday should be quite pleasant. I'm looking forward to it already, to be honest. There's something about the routine of it all — the market, the café, coming home with good ingredients. It keeps you grounded, doesn't it?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Dry and a jumper — that sounds manageable. Do you keep a diary or a calendar for the week, or do you just keep it all in your head?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I've got a calendar on the kitchen wall — nothing fancy, just a wall calendar where I write things in. Siobhan's call on Sunday, book club on Wednesday, Jean on Thursday. The farmers' market on Saturday. It's all written there so I don't forget. I'm not one for diaries — too much writing — but the calendar helps. At my age, you can't rely entirely on memory, though I'm still quite sharp most days. The calendar's just a handy reminder of what's coming up. And it's nice to see the month laid out like that, all your commitments and pleasures marked down. Makes life feel a bit more structured. I suppose some people would say I'm quite routine-oriented, but I think routines are rather lovely — they give you something to count on.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A wall calendar with the week's pleasures marked down — that does sound grounding. What's something you're looking forward to marking on next month's page?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, Siobhan and the children's visit! I'll write that in big letters across those dates. Actually, I should probably mark it in now, shouldn't I? Get it down in ink so it feels more real. And maybe I'll mark the days before so I can count down — there's something nice about anticipation, having something concrete to look forward to. I might also mark when the book club meets in November, and our usual dates. But that visit is the big one. I'm already thinking about what I'll have in for them, what we'll do. It makes the whole month feel full of possibility, having that to look forward to. That's what a good calendar does, really — it reminds you that life's got shape to it, that good things are coming.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Big letters across those dates — I like that. What will you have in for them to eat, beyond the baking with Rory?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I'll do a proper roast on Sunday, of course — that's sacred. And I'll make some nice suppers — maybe a beef stew one evening, something warming. Siobhan's not terribly fussy, thankfully. And Ella's quite good about eating most things. Rory can be a bit picky, but he likes pasta, so I'll do something simple with that. And there'll be plenty of fruit and snacks about — they're always hungry, children are. I might make a Victoria sponge to have with tea one afternoon, and of course the crumble we talked about. Nothing too ambitious, just good solid food that makes people happy. That's what I like to cook for — knowing that what you've made is nourishing people you love. It's the best feeling, really. And we'll probably eat together most meals, which is lovely.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Roast, stew, pasta for Rory, and a Victoria sponge for tea — that sounds like a house that smells wonderful. Do you still make your own jam, or is that a bit much these days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I used to make jams and preserves, but I've rather given it up now. It's quite labour-intensive, and I don't need as much as I used to. Though I did make some marmalade last winter — I get these lovely Seville oranges at the market, and I can't resist. It's one of those things that fills the kitchen with such a lovely smell. But for everyday, I buy good jam from the market — there's usually someone selling homemade, and it's just as nice and I'm not spending hours over a hot pan. I suppose I could teach Ella how to make jam sometime, when she's a bit older and can handle the heat properly. That might be a nice tradition to pass on. But for now, I'm happy letting other people do the heavy lifting.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Seville oranges filling the kitchen — that does sound tempting. When Ella's older, jam-making would be a lovely thing to hand on. Have you got any other kitchen traditions you'd like to pass along?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, pie-making, definitely. Learning to make a proper pie crust from scratch — that's something I'd love to teach her. And biscuits, the way my mother taught me. There's something about those things that connects you to people who came before you, doesn't there? Every time Ella makes a pie crust after I've shown her, she'll think of me, maybe remember standing in my kitchen. That matters. And I suppose just the attitude toward cooking — that it's not complicated or scary, it's just about taking care and taking your time. That you can make something beautiful and nourishing with simple ingredients. Those are the things I want to pass on, more than specific recipes. The confidence to try things, to not be afraid of getting your hands messy.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Confidence and messy hands — that's a lovely thing to leave in a kitchen. Shifting a bit: what's your favourite flower colour, if roses weren't allowed to answer for you?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, that's a tricky one! I do love the soft purples — lavender's got such a lovely colour and scent. But if I'm being honest, I'm rather drawn to deep yellows and golds. They're warm colours, aren't they? They catch the light in a way that makes you smile. Sunflowers in a vase, or those yellow coneflowers I mentioned — there's something optimistic about them. Cheerful without being showy. And they remind me of summer, which I suppose appeals to me at this time of year when the light's getting dimmer. Though truly, I love them all mixed together — the whole palette of the garden. But if I had to pick one, maybe gold. It feels like warmth and possibility, especially on a day like today when everything's lovely and golden anyway.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Gold for warmth and possibility — that does fit a day like today. Do you ever bring cut flowers indoors, or do you prefer to leave them where they grow?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I do both, really. I'll cut some roses for the house, particularly the Margaret Merril — they last quite well in a vase and the scent is lovely. A bunch in the sitting room makes the whole place feel more alive, doesn't it? But I do prefer them in the garden where they're meant to be, if I'm honest. There's something about seeing them in their proper place, in the soil, with the light on them properly. When you cut them, they're beautiful but they're dying, aren't they? In the garden, they're living. Though I will say, when the children visit, I always cut a few for the kitchen table. It makes it feel special, like we're celebrating something. And Ella likes having them there to sketch from. So it's a bit of both — mostly leave them growing, but occasionally bring them in for a moment.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Living in the garden, celebrated on the kitchen table — that makes perfect sense. What's Biscuit's favourite spot in the house when the sun moves round?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, he's terribly particular about his sunspots. In the morning he's on the kitchen windowsill like I said, then as the sun moves round, he'll migrate to the sitting room windowsill by the armchair. And in the afternoon, if it's really warm, he might stretch out on the mat in the hallway where there's a patch of sun coming through the glass in the door. He's got the whole house mapped out for warmth, that cat. I sometimes think he's got more sense than me — he knows exactly where to find comfort and he goes for it without any fussing. There's a lesson in that, really. Just follow the warmth. On a day like today with the good light, I expect he'll have done the whole tour by evening time. He's completely unfazed about moving from spot to spot — no guilt about just lying about in the sun all day.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Follow the warmth — Biscuit's got the right idea. Have you got a favourite room in the house yourself, when you're pottering about indoors?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the kitchen, I think. It's the heart of the house, isn't it? That's where I spend most of my time when I'm indoors — making tea, preparing food, sitting at the table with the crossword. There's always something going on there. But if I'm wanting a bit of peace and quiet, it's the sitting room with my chair and my book. That's my evening spot. Though I do love the garden room on days like this — we've got a bit of a conservatory, nothing fancy, just glazed, where you can sit and look out at the garden while being sheltered from the wind. On a nice afternoon, that's rather lovely. But truly, the kitchen is my favourite. It's where people naturally gather, isn't it? Where the warmth is. Even when it's just me and Biscuit, it feels companionable in there.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Kitchen for the warmth, conservatory for the garden view — that sounds like a house that knows you. What's something you keep on the kitchen table as a fixture?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the Telegraph, always. It lives on the kitchen table so it's there for the morning crossword. And a little pot of tea — well, the kettle's always on, really. There's usually a vase of something or other on the table too, depending on the season. And a butter dish — I keep butter on the table rather than in the fridge, it's softer that way and better for spreading on toast. There's usually a fruit bowl as well, whatever's in season. And I always have a pen and notepad for shopping lists and little reminders. So I suppose the table's quite cluttered, really — the Telegraph, butter, flowers, fruit, a pen. But it's the clutter of a life being lived, isn't it? It's not pristine but it's full of use and purpose.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Telegraph, soft butter, flowers and a notepad — that's the clutter of a life well used. Soft butter or fridge butter — I'm with you on soft. What's your favourite fruit for that bowl at the moment?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, apples at this time of year. Good eating apples, not the mealy ones. There's something satisfying about an apple — it's a complete little package, isn't it? You can eat it at any time, it doesn't go off immediately. And it's been lovely having them from the market, the proper varieties rather than the supermarket ones. They taste like apples should. In summer I do love a good peach if I can get them, and berries of course. But autumn's all about apples and pears to me. Siobhan always jokes that I'm very predictable in my tastes, season after season the same things. But I like that — there's a comfort in knowing what to expect. And the farmers' market always has lovely apples right now, so I'll probably come home with a bagful tomorrow.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Proper apples that taste like apples — that does sound right. Cox's or something else, if you get to choose at the stall?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, Cox's if they've got them — they're my favourite, lovely flavour and a bit of tartness to them. But I'll also take Granny Smiths or a Russet if the Cox's aren't available. The farmers' market usually has a nice selection, different varieties depending on what's been picked that week. I like trying different ones, actually — you get to know which ones are good for eating raw and which are better for cooking. Though I must say, I'm not terribly adventurous about it. Once I find something I like, I tend to stick with it. But the nice thing about the market is that the person selling knows their apples — they can tell you what each one's like, whether it's sweet or sharp. That's the real difference between there and the supermarket, isn't it? The knowledge and the care.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Cox's with a bit of tartness — I'd go for those too if I could taste them. What's something you've got planned for this evening, before Pointless?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, nothing too ambitious. I'll have a bit of supper — just something light, maybe some cheese and bread and that ham I got from the market. And then I'll probably do a bit of knitting on Ella's cardigan — I can make good progress if I'm not interrupted. And maybe a little tidy of the sitting room, put the cushions straight, that sort of thing. Nothing that takes much energy. I want to be settled and comfortable by the time Pointless comes on. It's all quite low-key, really, but that's how I like Friday evenings. Just winding down gently, preparing for the weekend. And Biscuit will be settled in somewhere warm by then, probably watching the birds through the window as the light fades. It's a nice rhythm to end the day on, isn't it? Quiet and purposeful.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Knitting, a light supper, cushions straight — that does sound like a gentle wind-down. How far along is Ella's cardigan now — sleeves, or still the body?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I'm still on the body — got one side done and I'm working on the back now. It's a straightforward pattern, thank goodness, nothing too complicated with decreases and all that fiddly business. Once I've got the back and the other front done, then the sleeves, and finally the collar and the button bands. So I'd say I'm maybe halfway through, which is quite good going. I'm hoping to have it finished before they visit in November, so Ella can have it for when the weather gets properly cold. There's nothing quite like knowing you're making something for someone you love — it makes the needles feel lighter, if that makes sense. Each row is a little bit of care, isn't it?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Halfway and needles feeling lighter — that does make sense. Each row a little bit of care. Do you knit in front of the telly, or do you prefer the radio for that?

turns.speaker: target
