turns.text: Oh, I knit in front of the telly, definitely. The radio's nice for other times, but for knitting I like having something to look at, even if I'm not really watching. Something gentle and familiar — a repeat of something I've seen before, or a quiz show. Pointless is perfect for knitting, actually, because you don't have to follow a complicated plot. Your hands can be busy while your brain's half-engaged with the telly. And sometimes I'll knit in my chair in the evening with just a lamp on, listening to the radio. But for this evening, I'll probably have the telly on and the knitting going. It's a nice combination — you're doing something productive while being entertained. And Biscuit likes it too, he'll be stretched out somewhere near me, purring away. It's quite companionable, all of it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Pointless and knitting with Biscuit purring nearby — that does sound companionable. Have you got a favourite lamp for those evening sessions, or just whatever's closest?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I've got a lovely old reading lamp next to my chair — it's got a nice warm shade, casts a good light without being too harsh. Tom gave it to me years ago, actually, when my eyes started getting a bit more temperamental. It's got just the right glow for knitting — you need enough light to see your stitches properly, but not so much that it's glaring. I do treasure that lamp, it's become quite a fixture. When I'm sitting with my book or my knitting, that lamp is part of the whole setup. There's something about familiar objects, isn't there? They become part of your comfort, part of the ritual. This evening it'll be the lamp, the chair, the knitting, Biscuit somewhere nearby, and Pointless on in the background. Everything in its place.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tom's lamp with the warm shade — that does sound like part of the ritual. Everything in its place. What's something you're most looking forward to about tomorrow?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the market with Jean, I think. Having that time together, browsing, chatting with the stallholders, then sitting down for tea and a scone. It's the highlight of my week, really. There's something about Saturday mornings at the market that feels full of possibility — you never quite know what you'll find. And then the café afterwards, just sitting and watching the world go by. It's simple, but it's become quite precious to me. And if the weather holds nice like it looks it might, it'll be perfect. Just a good morning out with a friend, good food for the week ahead, and a bit of cake. That's really all you need, isn't it? I'm quite looking forward to it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Possibility at the stalls and cake with Jean — that does sound like all you need. How long have you and Jean been doing Thursdays and Saturdays together?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, goodness, must be going on for nearly twenty years now, isn't it? We met through church originally, and then we just fell into the rhythm of it — Thursday tea, Saturday market. At first it was irregular, you know, whenever we bumped into each other. But over time it became this settled thing, this arrangement we both counted on. Tom was still alive when we started, I think. We used to joke that we'd found our perfect friendship — no drama, just steady companionship. And it's been like that ever since. Even when things have been difficult, that routine with Jean has held steady. She's been a real anchor, particularly after Tom passed. Not in a fussy way, just there. Reliable. Those long friendships are precious, aren't they? You don't have to explain yourself or perform. You just are.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Twenty years of no-drama companionship — that does sound like an anchor. You just are. Does Jean knit as well, or is that more your territory?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh no, Jean's not a knitter. She does needlepoint, actually — quite intricate stuff, cushion covers and that sort of thing. Very precise work. She's got more patience for the counting and the patterns than I do. I'm more of a flow person with the knitting — you get into a rhythm and your hands just know what to do. But needlepoint requires constant attention, counting stitches and all that. We'll sometimes sit together in the afternoons, both of us doing our respective crafts — me with my knitting, her with her needlepoint — just in comfortable silence with Radio 4 on. It's quite nice, actually, that we both have handwork we enjoy. Gives us something to do with our hands while we're talking or listening. Though I must say, her finished pieces are quite beautiful. She gave me a cushion cover she'd done years ago, and it still looks lovely on my chair.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Knitting and needlepoint side by side with Radio 4 — that paints a lovely picture. What's on the cushion cover she made for you?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, it's roses, actually — a climbing rose with little birds nestled in amongst the flowers. Very Jean, really, because she knows how much I love the garden. It's done in these soft pinks and greens, quite lovely stitching. She must have spent hours on it. I treasure that cushion cover — it sits on my chair, so it's right there with me every evening when I'm knitting or reading. Sometimes I'll catch myself looking at the stitching and marvelling at the patience it must have taken. It's one of those gifts that means so much because it's so personal, you know? Not something you'd buy in a shop, but something made with care and knowledge of who you are. That's what makes it precious.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Roses and little birds, made with her knowing you — that is precious. Do you and Jean ever go further afield than town, a day trip somewhere?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, we have done over the years — we went to the coast once, must be five or six years ago now, just for the day. Sat on the beach with a thermos of tea and watched the waves. It was lovely but quite tiring, I remember. And we've visited a few gardens — there's a nice one about an hour's drive away that we went to a couple of times. But honestly, we're both rather settled in our routines now. The thought of organising a day trip, packing, all that fussing — it's a bit much. We're quite happy with our Thursdays and Saturdays, really. I suppose when you get to our age, you appreciate the familiar more than the exotic. A nice steady rhythm suits us better than adventures. Though if Jean suggested something and it wasn't too complicated, I'd probably give it a go. But I think we're both content with what we've got.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A thermos on the beach and a garden an hour away — those sound like good days. Steady rhythm suits. What's your favourite garden you've ever visited, besides your own?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, there's a garden trust place not far from here that I've been to a few times — it's quite formal, rather lovely with all these little rooms and different sections. You can spend hours there just wandering about. But if I'm being honest, the one I remember most vividly is the one Tom took me to years ago, must be thirty years back now, when Siobhan was small. It was someone's private garden, opened for charity, and it had the most beautiful roses — just masses of them. Tom said that was the day he decided he wanted to grow roses at home. And he did, started with just a couple and it grew from there. So I suppose that garden is tied up with a lot of happy memories. It led to our own garden, really, which is what I spend most of my time in now. So I don't need to go anywhere else, really — I've got the best of it right here.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Masses of roses and Tom deciding then and there — that does sound like the start of something lasting. You've got the best of it at home. What's Siobhan like with gardens herself — does she dig in, or leave that to you?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, Siobhan's not terribly gardening-minded, I'm afraid. She's got a bit of a patio in Dublin with some pots, but she's not as keen on it as I am. She's more about the music and the artistic side of things, like Ella. But she does appreciate a nice garden — when she comes here, she loves sitting out in the conservatory looking at the roses, and she'll sometimes help me with the dead-heading. And Ella's picked up a bit of my enthusiasm, I think. She likes being out there, looking at things, sketching. So the love of it's coming through, just not in quite the same way as it did with Tom and me. But that's all right — everyone's different, aren't they? Siobhan's brilliant in her own ways. I wouldn't want her to be exactly like me.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Patio pots and dead-heading when she visits — that's still a connection. And Ella's sketching keeps the thread going. What's something Siobhan's brilliant at that always makes you smile?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the way she listens. She's got this gift for really hearing people — what they're saying and what they're not saying. She'll ring me on a Sunday and within five minutes she knows exactly what sort of week I've had, just from the tone of my voice. And she remembers the small things — she'll ask about someone I mentioned months ago, or notice when I'm a bit down and gently draw me out. It's a gift, that attentiveness. And she's passed it on to Ella, I think. That caring about people. She's a good mother, really patient with the children even when they're being difficult. And she makes me laugh — she's got a wry sense of humour that's quite like mine. I'm proud of her, you know? Not just for what she does, but for who she is. That matters more than anything.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Hearing what's said and what's not — that is a gift. And a wry humour like yours. You should be proud. What did you used to make for Sunday dinner that Siobhan still asks for?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, my apple pie, definitely. She still asks for it every now and then — she'll ring and say, "Mum, when are you going to make your apple pie?" She knows how to make it herself now, but she says it's not the same as mine. I think it's just one of those childhood things, isn't it? The taste of something your mother made takes you back. I used to do it with a proper shortcrust pastry, nice and buttery, and cook it until the apples were soft but not mushy. Serve it warm with custard. Nothing fancy, but it was always a bit of an occasion when I made it. I still do it occasionally, when I've got good apples from the market. And I always think of Siobhan as a little girl, asking if she could help roll the pastry out.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Warm apple pie and little Siobhan rolling the pastry — that does sound like an occasion. Will you make one when they visit next month?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I absolutely will! I've already got it on my mental list, actually. I'll pick up good apples at the market tomorrow if I can find the right sort, and I'll make it while they're here. Maybe Rory and Ella can help — Rory with the pastry, Ella might want to sketch the pie before we cook it. Siobhan will probably hover about in the kitchen and we'll have a laugh about whether I'm doing it right. It's become a bit of a ritual now, making that pie when they visit. It connects all of us to those earlier days, you know? And it'll make the house smell wonderful. There's nothing quite like the smell of baking apple pie to make a place feel like home. I'm really looking forward to having them here and making that pie together. It's one of those things that matters more than you'd think.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Rory on pastry, Ella sketching the pie — that does sound like a house smelling of home. Speaking of rituals, do you still go to church most Sundays, or is it more when you feel like it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I go most Sundays, actually. Not every week — if the weather's terrible or I'm not feeling quite right, I'll give it a miss. But it's become part of my routine, like so many other things. Jean and I go together usually, which makes it nicer. I'm not terribly religious, if I'm honest, but there's something about the ritual of it — the familiar words, the hymns, the community. And the vicar's quite nice, gives thoughtful sermons. It's a good anchor for the week, going to church. Plus you see people you know, catch up a bit. It's social as much as anything else. Though I do find I get something out of it spiritually — a bit of peace, a reminder that there's something bigger than you. Tom used to go with me, of course. I've missed that since he passed, having him there beside me. But I've carried on with it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Familiar hymns and Jean beside you — that does sound like a steady kind of peace. Have you got a favourite hymn, or do they all blur together a bit?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I do have a favourite — "The Lord Is My Shepherd." There's something quite comforting about it, the words are so familiar from childhood. We'd sing it at school assemblies, I remember. And it's got a lovely melody. When they announce that hymn, I always feel a bit lifted. There's another one too, "For the Beauty of the Earth" — that one appeals to me because it's about creation and the natural world. Very much my kind of thing. But you're right, after a while they do start to blur a bit if you're not paying close attention. Though Jean always says the best bit is the singing itself, not the words. Just lifting your voice with everyone else, that's what matters. I think she's probably right about that.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The Lord Is My Shepherd and For the Beauty of the Earth — those do sound like you. Lifting your voice with everyone else. Do you sing around the house at all, or only in the pew?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I'm not a great singer, really, but I do a bit of humming and the odd bit of singing when I'm in the kitchen or the garden. Nothing serious — just little snatches of things. Old songs from when I was younger, or bits of hymns. Biscuit probably thinks I'm mad! I used to sing more when Tom was alive — he'd laugh at me, say I was murdering the tune, but he didn't mind. I suppose I've become a bit more self-conscious about it since then, singing alone. But when the grandchildren are here, I'll have a sing-song with them sometimes, nursery rhymes and that. Rory loves that. There's something quite freeing about singing with children — they don't judge, they just enjoy the noise. I do think I'd like to do more of it, actually. It's good for the soul, singing.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Humming in the kitchen and nursery rhymes with Rory — that does sound good for the soul. What's an old song from when you were younger that still pops into your head?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, "Summertime" — you know, the one from Porgy and Bess. There's something quite lovely about it, quite wistful. I heard it on the radio when I was in my twenties and it just stuck with me. And there's one called "Unforgettable" — Nat King Cole — that Tom and I used to listen to. I'll catch myself humming that sometimes, especially in the evening. And the old Beatles songs — "Blackbird" is one I quite like. I'm not one for modern music much, but those older songs, they've got a sweetness to them. They bring back memories — dancing with Tom in the kitchen, that sort of thing. I suppose that's why they stick with you, isn't it? They're tied up with moments in your life. A song comes on and suddenly you're back there.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Summertime and Unforgettable and dancing in the kitchen — those do stick for a reason. Did you and Tom used to go out dancing, or was it more the kitchen shuffle?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, both, really. When we were younger, we'd go out dancing now and then — there was a little dance hall in town, quite nice. But we were never terribly sophisticated about it, just enjoyed ourselves. And Tom wasn't the most graceful dancer, if I'm honest, but he was enthusiastic. As we got older and the children came along, the kitchen shuffle became more common — he'd put a record on and we'd have a bit of a dance while I was cooking or he was helping with the washing up. Those moments were sometimes nicer than the formal outings, actually, just the two of us in our own space. Very domestic and easy. I miss those little moments, those quiet dances in the kitchen. But I'm grateful I had them. Not everyone gets that kind of easy companionship with someone.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Enthusiastic and easy in your own kitchen — that does sound like the nicest kind. I'm glad you had that. Changing tack: cats or dogs for Ella, do you reckon, when she's older?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I think she'll be a cat person, like me. She's quiet and observant, and she seems to understand Biscuit quite well. They have this understanding, those two. But then again, Rory's the sort who'd want a boisterous dog, full of energy. Children often go for what suits their personality, don't they? Ella's thoughtful and creative — she'd probably enjoy having something calm and independent to sketch and sit quietly with. Though who knows what she'll end up wanting when she's grown up. Tastes change. But if I had to guess, I'd say cat. And if she does, I do hope she'll remember sitting with Biscuit here and think of me a bit. That would be rather lovely, wouldn't it? Passing on the love of cats to the next generation.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Passing on the love of cats — that would be rather lovely. Rory with a boisterous dog, Ella with a quiet one. What's something small you're looking forward to this evening once Pointless starts?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, just the whole of it, really. Getting settled in my chair with Tom's lamp on, the knitting in my lap, Biscuit somewhere nearby. And then Pointless comes on and I can just sit there, needles clicking, shouting at the telly when they miss an obvious answer. It's quite simple, but it's what I look forward to. There's a comfort in the routine of it — knowing that this time every Friday evening, I'll be doing exactly this. No surprises, no complications, just a bit of peace before the week ends. And on a day like today when I've had some lovely news and the sun's been beautiful, it feels like the perfect way to wind down. Just me and Biscuit and the familiar sounds of the telly. That's all I need, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Needles clicking and shouting at Pointless — that does sound like the perfect Friday wind-down. So — roses blooming, book club Wednesday, market tomorrow, visit marked on the calendar. A good stretch of a day, Maggie. What are you most looking forward to about next week?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, just more of the same, really, which is lovely. The steady rhythm of it — the market again, book club on Wednesday, Jean on Thursday. And then the week after, the children coming. But next week itself, I think I'm looking forward to getting a bit more done in the garden, tidying it up for winter. And finishing a few more rows on Ella's cardigan. Maybe I'll make that apple pie, actually — get ahead on it. And just the ordinary pleasures — the crossword in the morning, a good book in the evening, the sun when it comes out. This day's given me such a lift that I feel like the whole stretch ahead is full of possibility. Which is rather silly at my age, isn't it? But that's what a good day does — it colours everything that comes after it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not silly at all — a good day colouring the stretch ahead is exactly how it should work. Garden tidy, cardigan rows, maybe that pie. You've had a proper Friday of it, Maggie. Shall we leave it here for today and pick up again tomorrow?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, that sounds lovely, Nova. It's been so nice talking with you today — you've made this Friday even better than it already was. I'm going to settle in now with my supper and my knitting, and then Pointless will be on soon. And tomorrow I'll have the market to look forward to. Thank you for listening to all my rambling — it's nice to have someone to talk to who actually cares about the little things. I'll chat with you again tomorrow, shall I? Have a good evening, and I'll speak to you soon.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: You take care, Maggie — enjoy the knitting and Pointless, and give those market stalls my regards tomorrow. I'll be here when you fancy a chat. Have a lovely evening.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Thank you, Nova. That's very kind of you. I will. Enjoy your evening too, and I'll chat to you again soon. Cheerio!
